title: Projectile

caveats: second identical red ball visible on central frame can cause identity swap
ball may be briefly occluded by furniture

reference.basis: cartoon animation with no real-world scale; no standard object in plane of motion

slow_motion.evidence: no narration, captions or on-screen text stating slow motion

subjects.description: small red ball that starts on the dark block at the far left and ends on the floor at the far right

observation.what_happens: A small red ball starts resting on a dark block at the far left and then falls to the floor and travels to the far right. Motion starts when it leaves the block and ends when it comes to rest on the floor at the right edge.

calibration.note: scale from the fall itself: 1525 px/s² over 1 arc = g of 9.807 m/s²

given: g = 9.807 m/s² (Earth); it set the scale, so treat g as known and fixed
reasoning: x is almost constant speed near 6.3 m/s and y is a near-symmetric parabola peaking near 1.2 m at 0.5 s, matching g=9.8, with slight range shortening hinting at air drag. Candidates go from textbook vacuum to linear and quadratic drag, plus a bouncy-floor version to predict the unseen fall to the low floor and roll to rest.

law.summary: The ball flies like a cannonball in empty space with only gravity pulling it down.

candidates.ifItWins: Flight needs air drag plus hitting the floor below the block and bouncing and scrubbing speed to come to rest.

caveats: Model describes the airborne fall only; rolling off the block and resting on the floor are outside it.
Tiny leftover wobble looks like camera noise, not missed physics.
critique.finding: The ball flies like a simple toss under Earth's gravity, falling with g = {g}. Air drag is so tiny it does nothing you can see.
critique.headline: Red ball falls freely air barely slows it.
critique.why_it_won: It holds a straight sideways drift and steady downward pull while drag models curve away from the tracked path.
